meta.title: Who really said "Give me four years to teach the children, and the seed I have sown shall never be uprooted"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited to Lenin, but this exact line first shows up in Bruce Hopper's 1931 book Pan-Sovietism, with no source. No Lenin text containing it has been found.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Give me four years to teach the children, and the seed I have sown shall never be uprooted'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Lenin, but the wording first appears in a 1931 American book with no source, and early versions disagree. Here is the paper trail.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Lenin, but nobody has found it in his speeches or writings. Every early version is second-hand and printed after his death, and the versions disagree. This exact wording appears in Bruce Hopper’s Pan-Sovietism (1931), p. 87, which says only “It was Lenin who said” and gives no source.

source.heading: Where the wording first appears

docMeta.dd: Pan-Sovietism: The Issue Before America and the World
Bruce Hopper (from his 1931 Lowell Institute lectures)
Boston and New York: Houghton Mifflin, 1931 · p. 87
None. Hopper says only “It was Lenin who said”

source.excerpt: The general result is a growing mass of youth, trained in politics, economics and social welfare, and trained to be useful to society and the interests of the proletarian class. The younger groups also make a virtue of good manners. It was Lenin who said: ‘Give me four years to teach the children, and the seed I have sown shall never be uprooted.’ These leaders of tomorrow in Russia are the product of Communist civic training.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ lists the line under “Attributions” on its Lenin page. It cites only Bruce Campbell Hopper’s Pan-Sovietism (Houghton Mifflin, 1931), p. 87, and names no Lenin work.
The Internet Archive scan of Pan-Sovietism ↗ shows the sentence on p. 87, in a passage about the Komsomol and the Pioneers, with no source given.

Barry Popik ↗ finds that the earliest printed versions date from the late 1920s and early 1930s, after Lenin’s death, and that they vary. His earliest is a 1929 line, “Give me four years with the children, and I do not care what happens.” He records the “seed I have sown” wording in 1931, in Hopper’s What Russia Intends (London: Cape), p. 83.
source.excerptNote: Hopper presents the line as something Lenin said and names no speech, article or date. The wording is Hopper’s English, and no Russian original has been identified.

source.rightsNote: This exact English wording is first documented in Bruce Hopper’s Pan-Sovietism, published in the United States in 1931 with the notice “Copyright, 1931, by Bruce C. Hopper.” Under a conservative reading, a 1931 U.S. publication is treated as still in copyright in 2026. Because no Lenin original has been identified, there is no older public-domain text to fall back on.

author.name: Vladimir Lenin
author.heading: About Vladimir Lenin
author.bio: Vladimir Ilyich Lenin (born Ulyanov) led the Bolsheviks to power in the October Revolution of 1917. He headed the Soviet state until he died in January 1924. His works fill many volumes of Collected Works, and the line credited to him here has not been traced to any of them.

misattribution.heading: Why the Lenin credit is shaky
misattribution.intro: This is not a proven fabrication, and nobody has named a different author. But no Lenin text is known to contain it, and every early report is second-hand, printed after his death and worded differently:

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ files it under “Attributions” and cites only Hopper’s 1931 book, not anything Lenin wrote. Hopper himself gives no source.
“Lenin once said, ‘Give me four years with the children, and I do not care what happens.’” This is the earliest citation in Popik’s list ↗, and it has no “seed” at all.
“Give me four years in which to teach the children, and my clock will never be put back.” This appeared in the same year as Hopper’s version, per Popik ↗.
“Give me,” said he, “five years to teach the children and the seed sown shall not be uprooted.” Woody also compares Lenin to Erasmus, per Popik ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The best-documented early source for this exact wording is Bruce Hopper’s Pan-Sovietism (1931), p. 87 ↗. It is hearsay: Hopper gives no source, and the versions printed around the same time disagree on the details.

context.heading: Why it caught on
lead: The line spread through Western books about Soviet Russia around 1930, when visitors were struck by how the regime organized the young. Hopper uses it in a passage about the Komsomol, the Pioneers and the Little Octobrists, the Communist youth groups that trained children from infancy. He calls them “leaders of tomorrow” who represent “disciplined power, obedient to the central will.”

The saying fits Lenin’s known emphasis on educating a new generation, which is one reason it stuck. But fitting someone’s views is not evidence that he said it. The early versions disagree on four years or five, and on whether the seed “shall never be uprooted” or whether his “clock will never be put back.” That variation is typical of a saying passed along by word of mouth, not copied from a text.
